title: The Discovery of Pluto
passages: In 1930, a 24-year-old named Clyde Tombaugh was working at Lowell OBSERVATORY in Flagstaff, Arizona. He had grown up on a farm in Kansas and had no college degree, but he built his own telescopes. His job was to hunt for a hidden "Planet X." He compared pairs of photographs of the night sky using a machine called a blink COMPARATOR, which flipped quickly between two images. On February 18, 1930, he spotted a tiny dot that had moved between pictures taken six days apart. The discovery was announced on March 13, 1930.

Pluto is very far away. On average it sits about 5.9 billion kilometers (3.7 billion miles) from the Sun, nearly 40 times farther than Earth. Its path is a stretched oval, or ELLIPTICAL orbit, so the distance changes from roughly 4.4 to more than 7.3 billion kilometers. Sunlight takes about five and a half hours to reach it. The name came from Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, England, who suggested the Roman god of the underworld. In Japan, writer Hoei Nojiri offered Meiōsei, meaning "star of the king of the underworld," a name also used in China and Korea. In 2006, astronomers RECLASSIFIED Pluto as a dwarf planet.
